result.note: Corporate deal with a policy angle; tested Vizhinjam's ownership and concession structure and its geographic advantages as a transhipment hub.

questions.prompt: In July 2026, Adani Ports agreed to sell a 49% stake in the company operating Vizhinjam Port to MSC Group. Consider the following statements about Vizhinjam Port:
items: It is owned by the Government of Kerala through a state entity, Vizhinjam International Seaport Limited.
Adani runs it under a 40-year build-operate-transfer concession held by a subsidiary.
Under the concession agreement, only an ownership change above 49% needs the Kerala government's approval.
questions.ask: Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explain: Statement 3 is wrong because the concession requires Kerala's approval for any ownership change above 25%, so the 49% sale needs the state's consent. The deal values the hub at USD 2.85 billion and is the largest foreign private investment in Indian port infrastructure.
questions.source: Under the concession agreement, any ownership change above 25% needs the Kerala government's approval, and as the asset's owner the state has a real say.

questions.prompt: Consider the following statements about Kerala's Vizhinjam Port, as described in July 2026:
items: It sits about 10 nautical miles off the main east-west shipping lane.
Its natural draft of 18 to 20 metres needs no dredging.
questions.ask: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.explain: Both are correct. Vizhinjam is India's only deep-water terminal directly on the main east-west lane, and its depth lets it take mega-vessels most Indian ports cannot. Roughly 75% of India's transhipment cargo is currently routed through Colombo, Singapore and Jebel Ali.
questions.source: The port is India's only deep-water terminal sitting directly on the main east-west shipping lane, about 10 nautical miles off it, with an 18 to 20 metre natural draft that needs no dredging.
